title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu
openingText: These are the teachings of Master Sun. For every nation, war is a matter of immense importance. The army determines whether people live or die: through it the State survives or is destroyed. It therefore demands careful and sustained study. In warfare, alongside strategy and circumstances, five things are essential. They are named, in order, The Way, Heaven, Earth, the Leader, and Law. None of these five can be left out.
about:
The Art of War is a Chinese work on military strategy attributed to Sun Tzu. Its thirteen chapters examine planning, supplies, command, morale, terrain, deception and intelligence. Its recurring question is how to secure victory without wasting the army or exhausting the state. Winning without fighting is the ideal, but much of the book concerns what to do when fighting cannot be avoided.

Tinct's original English edition is E. F. Calthrop's 1908 translation in The Book of War. The modern English and Danish editions follow that text. They preserve its historical examples and often uncompromising instructions, including commands to deceive, plunder and punish. These are the arguments of the historical work, not advice from Tinct.

Reading note: two apparent errors in Calthrop are corrected in both modern editions, with support from Lionel Giles's 1910 translation. In chapter VII, paragraph 26, rested troops face a tired enemy, rather than the reverse. In chapter VIII, paragraph 6, knowledge of the Five Advantages is useless if the Nine Changes are not understood. The original edition retains Calthrop's wording. Terrain and spy categories are described more directly in Danish. Historical distance and money units are retained without conversion to kilometres or modern currency.

angleCards.title: Winning without fighting
angleCards.text: Follow the preference for victory without battle. How does it shape planning, alliances and the use of force?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how the ideal of winning without battle shapes the book's practical instructions.

angleCards.title: Knowledge and deception
angleCards.text: Track what the commander must know, what the enemy must be made to believe, and what the soldiers must not be told.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the relationship between intelligence, deception and trust.

angleCards.title: The cost of war
angleCards.text: Look at the passages on food, money, exhaustion and civilian livelihoods. What limits do these place on military ambition?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the book's account of the material and human costs of war.

angleCards.title: Beyond the battlefield
angleCards.text: Test an idea against a decision outside war. Where does the comparison help, and where does the military setting make it misleading?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test possible applications outside war without losing sight of the original military context.

cast.name: Sun Tzu
cast.description: Each chapter presents the master's teaching. The text moves between short rules, comparisons and explanations of how a commander should act.

cast.name: The commander
cast.description: The commander studies the enemy and the terrain, manages troops and supplies, and decides when to fight. Military judgment may require disobeying the ruler.

cast.name: The ruler
cast.description: The ruler issues commands and bears responsibility for the state. The book warns against interference based on ignorance of the army's situation and against war undertaken in anger.

cast.name: The enemy
cast.description: The enemy's numbers, preparedness, morale, supplies and movements must be understood. Underestimating the enemy is presented as a route to defeat.

cast.name: The terrain
cast.description: Different ground creates different opportunities and dangers. The book distinguishes terrain by access, retreat, distance, supply and the pressure it places on soldiers.

cast.name: The spies
cast.description: The final chapter distinguishes five kinds of spies. It stresses their pay, secrecy and treatment, and gives a central role to enemy agents brought into one's own service.

whyItMatters.title: Victory and restraint
whyItMatters.body: The book ranks capturing a country intact above defeating it by fire and sword. Its preference for winning without battle sits alongside detailed instructions for fighting. Reading those together shows what its ideal demands and where it gives way to necessity.

whyItMatters.title: Command under pressure
whyItMatters.body: A commander must judge changing circumstances rather than follow every order mechanically. Anger, rashness, excessive caution and concern for reputation can undermine that judgment.

whyItMatters.title: War depends on resources
whyItMatters.body: The opening chapters connect military operations to food, money and the burden on households. The final chapter returns to the cost of ignorance: refusing to pay for intelligence can waste far more than it saves.
